Before the city fully wakes, there is a brief interval when every sound seems chosen: a shutter lifting, a kettle sighing, tires whispering over rain. I like that hour because it asks nothing from me except attention, and attention feels less like effort than a heavy door quietly opening inward. Most days, I move through the world collecting evidence for arguments I never meant to make, mistaking hurry for purpose and noise for good company. Yet a single unhurried look can interrupt the pattern: light on a windowsill, steam curling above a cup, a stranger patiently holding a door open. Such details do not solve anything, but they return the world to its proper size, large enough for wonder and still small enough for tenderness.

Perhaps wisdom begins there, not with answers, but with the decision to notice what remains after our restless explanations have exhausted themselves and finally departed. I do not mean that life becomes gentle simply because I watch it closely; grief remains grief, and difficult work still waits in the morning. But attention gives me somewhere honest to stand, a place from which I can answer sorrow without adding needless cruelty to its already considerable weight. Tomorrow will likely sweep me back into urgency, and I will forget the shutter, the kettle, the patient hand, the almost silver light of dawn. Still, forgetting is not failure; it is simply another chance to return, to look again, and to be surprised by what was waiting all along.
